senses.definition: Electromagnetic radiation in the wavelength range visible to the human eye (about 400–750 nanometers): visible light.
senses.example: As you can see, this spacious dining-room gets a lot of light in the mornings.

senses.definition: Electromagnetic radiation in the wavelength range visible to the human eye or in nearby ranges (infrared or ultraviolet radiation).
senses.example: black light

senses.definition: Electromagnetic radiation of any wavelength.
senses.example: It’s everywhere. At this moment, as you sit quietly reading this book, you are awash in it. At work, it’s emanating from your electronic devices; step outside for lunch, and the sun bathes you in it. You may receive an extra dose of it when you visit your doctor, pass through security at the airport, or drive through city streets, but minuscule amounts of it are with you always. You cannot see, hear, smell, or feel it, but there is never a single second when it is not flying through your body. Too much of it will kill you, but without it you wouldn’t live a year. “Invisible light” seems like a contradiction. Like Simon and Garfunkel’s “The Sound of Silence,” it’s an oxymoron. We think of light, by definition, as something seen, something that enables our seeing, illuminating the darkness. Unlike dogs, who sniff in order to “get” what an object is, we depend on vision above all our other senses. We rely on light to tell us about our surroundings. But just as there are frequencies of sound audible to other animals that we cannot hear, there is a whole world of light outside our range of vision, a world that is humming with activity. Though we rarely think about this invisible world, our way of life depends on it. It’s because of invisible light that you can do things such as send a text message, use GPS to find your way to a friend’s house, listen to the radio, or microwave a frozen pizza. Invisible light shows us things we would never otherwise see, including our own skeletons and brains and the history of our universe. I was reminded of just how much we rely on invisible light, and how mysterious it remains to us, during a visit from my sister and her family. It was a lazy summer afternoon, and we were sprawled across a few couches sharing a bowl of popcorn. My niece, her shoulders crimson after a day outdoors, was chatting on her cell phone, holding up a promising finger to her mother, who was scolding her for not using sunscreen. My brother-in-law, meanwhile, was asking my opinion on an article he’d read proposing that Wi-Fi be banned in schools because of its dangers. We were all depending on invisible light (for the microwave popcorn, the cell-phone service) while being concerned that it might harm us (sunburn, mysterious Wi-Fi health threats) and confused about what to do to protect ourselves. We need it, and it surrounds us, yet we remain uneasy about living with invisible light, partly because we fear what is unknown. After all, most of us don’t know much about “all the light we cannot see.” This book aims to change that. My hope is to expose the hidden side of the spectrum, to make the invisible (at least temporarily) visible and vivid to you.

senses.definition: A source of illumination.
senses.example: Put that light out!

senses.definition: Spiritual or mental illumination; enlightenment, useful information.
senses.example: Can you throw any light on this problem?

senses.definition: Facts; pieces of information; ideas, concepts.
senses.example: Now these notions are twofold, actions or habits[…], which are durable lights and notions, which we may use when we will.

senses.definition: A notable person within a specific field or discipline.
senses.example: Picasso was one of the leading lights of the cubist movement.

senses.definition: The manner in which the light strikes a picture; that part of a picture which represents those objects upon which the light is supposed to fall; the more illuminated part of a landscape or other scene; opposed to shade.
A point of view, or aspect from which a concept, person or thing is regarded.
senses.example: I'm really seeing you in a different light today.

senses.definition: A flame or something used to create fire.
senses.example: "There will, I expect, be many such - possibly whole cities in flames - when we consider how many folk may have dropped with lights in their hands."

senses.definition: A firework made by filling a case with a substance which burns brilliantly with a white or coloured flame.
senses.example: a Bengal light

senses.definition: A window in architecture, carriage design, or motor car design: either the opening itself or the window pane of glass that fills it, if any.
senses.example: This facade has eight south-facing lights.

senses.definition: The series of squares reserved for the answer to a crossword clue.
senses.example: The average length of a light on a 15×15 grid is 7 or 8.

senses.definition: A cross-light in a double acrostic or triple acrostic.
Open view; a visible state or condition; public observation; publicity.
senses.example: The duke yet would have dark deeds darkly answered; he would never bring them to light.

senses.definition: The power of perception by vision: eyesight (sightedness; vision).
senses.example: My heart panteth, my strength faileth me: as for the light of mine eies, it also is gone from me.

senses.definition: The brightness of the eye or eyes.
senses.example: He seemed to find his way without his eyes; / For out o'door he went without their helps, / And, to the last, bended their light on me.

senses.definition: To start (a fire).
senses.example: We lit the fire to get some heat.

senses.definition: To set fire to; to set burning.
senses.example: She lit her last match.

senses.definition: To illuminate; to provide light for when it is dark.
senses.example: I used my torch to light the way home through the woods in the night.

senses.definition: To become ignited; to take fire.
senses.example: This soggy match will not light.

senses.definition: To attend or conduct with a light; to show the way to by means of a light.
senses.example: His bishops lead him forth, and light him on.

senses.definition: To make (a bonus) available to be collected by hitting a target, and thus light up the feature light corresponding to that bonus to indicate its availability.
senses.example: Light the extra ball by amassing 500 million points in the wizard mode.

senses.definition: Having light; bright; clear; not dark or obscure.
senses.example: The room is light when the Sun shines through the window.

senses.definition: Pale or whitish in color; highly luminous and more or less deficient in chroma.
senses.example: She had light skin.

senses.definition: Served with extra milk or cream.
senses.example: Do you want your coffee light or black? -I like mine light.

senses.definition: Having little or relatively little actual weight; not heavy; not cumbrous or unwieldy.
senses.example: a light load ; a lighter backpack after having removed the books ; light weapons

senses.definition: Having little weight as compared with bulk; of little density or specific gravity.
senses.example: feathers and cork are light ; oil is lighter than water

senses.definition: Of short or insufficient weight; weighing less than the legal, standard, or proper amount; clipped or diminished.
senses.example: to issue light coin

senses.definition: Lacking that which burdens or makes heavy.
Not heavy or soggy; spongy; well raised.
senses.example: a light bread ; sponge cake is a light cake

senses.definition: Low in fat, calories, alcohol, salt, etc.
senses.example: This light beer still gets you drunk if you have enough of it.

senses.definition: Slight, not forceful or intense; small in amount or intensity.
senses.example: a light drizzle//a light rain was falling//a light snow set in

senses.definition: Gentle; having little force or momentum.
senses.example: This artist clearly had a light, flowing touch.

senses.definition: Easy to endure or perform.
senses.example: light duties around the house

senses.definition: Unimportant, trivial, having little value or significance.
senses.example: I made some light comment, and we moved on.

senses.definition: Unchaste, wanton.
senses.example: Long after lay he musing at her mood, / Much grieu'd to thinke that gentle Dame so light, / For whose defence he was to shed his blood.

senses.definition: Not encumbered; unembarrassed; clear of impediments; hence, active; nimble; swift.
senses.example: Unmarried men are best friends, best masters […] but not always best subjects, for they are light to run away.

senses.definition: Fast; nimble.
Easily influenced by trifling considerations; unsteady; unsettled; volatile.
senses.example: a light, vain person; a light mind

senses.definition: Indulging in, or inclined to, levity; lacking dignity or solemnity; frivolous; airy.
senses.example: Ogden Nash was a writer of light verse.

senses.definition: Not quite sound or normal; somewhat impaired or deranged; dizzy; giddy.
senses.example: Are his wits safe? Is he not light of brain?

senses.definition: Easily interrupted by stimulation.
senses.example: light sleep; light anesthesia

senses.definition: Cheerful.
senses.example:
I wish you a good day, and you'll find a way
 To make your spirits light & gay

senses.definition: Carrying little.
senses.example: I prefer to travel light.

senses.definition: A stone that is not thrown hard enough.
See lights (“lungs”).
A low-alcohol lager.
senses.example: We crossed to the pub on the corner of Carlisle Street and I ordered two schooners of old for him and one of light for me.

senses.definition: A member of the light cavalry.
To unload a ship, or to jettison material to make it lighter.
To lighten; to ease of a burden; to take off.
senses.example: His mailèd habergeon she did undight, / And from his head his heavy burgonet did light.

senses.definition: To leave; to depart.
To find by chance.
senses.example: I lit upon a rare book in a second-hand bookseller's.

senses.definition: To stop upon (of eyes or a glance); to notice.
senses.example: "Sacredam!" he cried, when his eyes lit upon Buck. "Dat one dam bully dog! Eh? How moch?"

senses.definition: To alight; to land or come down.
senses.example: She fell out of the window but luckily lit on her feet.

senses.definition: Honorific alternative letter-case form of light, sometimes used when referring to God or another important figure who is understood from context.
A surname.
A place name:
The 24th sura (chapter) of the Qur'an.
